1 sn Job answers Eliphaz, but not until he introduces new ideas for his own case with God. His speech unfolds in three parts: Job&apos;s longing to meet God (23:2-7), the inaccessibility and power of God (23:8-17), the indifference of God (24:1-25).

2 tc The MT reads here מְרִי (mÿri, &quot;rebellious&quot;). The word is related to the verb מָרָה (marah, &quot;to revolt&quot;). Many commentators follow the Vulgate, Targum Job, and the Syriac to read מַר (mar, &quot;bitter&quot;). The LXX offers no help here. 3 tc The MT (followed by the Vulgate and Targum) has &quot;my hand is heavy on my groaning.&quot; This would mean &quot;my stroke is heavier than my groaning&quot; (an improbable view from Targum Job). A better suggestion is that the meaning would be that Job tries to suppress his groans but the hand with which he suppresses them is too heavy (H. H. Rowley, Job [NCBC], 159). Budde, E. Dhorme, J. E. Hartley, and F. I. Andersen all maintain the MT as the more difficult reading. F. I. Andersen (Job [TOTC], 208) indicates that the ִי(i) suffix could be an example of an unusual third masculine singular. Both the LXX and the Syriac versions have &quot;his hand,&quot; and many modern commentators follow this, along with the present translation. In this case the referent of &quot;his&quot; would be God, whose hand is heavy upon Job in spite of Job&apos;s groaning. 4 tn The preposition can take this meaning; it could be also translated simply &quot;upon.&quot; R. Gordis (Job, 260) reads the preposition &quot;more than,&quot; saying that Job had been defiant (he takes that view) but God&apos;s hand had been far worse.

5 tn The optative here is again expressed with the verbal clause, &quot;who will give [that] I knew....&quot; 6 tn The form in Hebrew is וְאֶמְצָאֵהוּ (vÿ&apos;emtsa&apos;ehu), simply &quot;and I will find him.&quot; But in the optative clause this verb is subordinated to the preceding verb: &quot;O that I knew where [and] I might find him.&quot; It is not unusual to have the perfect verb followed by the imperfect in such coordinate clauses (see GKC 386 §120.e). This could also be translated making the second verb a complementary infinitive: &quot;knew how to find him.&quot; sn H. H. Rowley (Job [NCBC], 159) quotes Strahan without reference: &quot;It is the chief distinction between Job and his friends that he desires to meet God and they do not.&quot; 7 tn This verb also depends on מִי־יִתֵּן (mi-yitten, &quot;who will give&quot;) of the first part, forming an additional clause in the wish formula. 8 tn Or &quot;his place of judgment.&quot; The word is from כּוּן (kun, &quot;to prepare; to arrange&quot;) in the Polel and the Hiphil conjugations. The noun refers to a prepared place, a throne, a seat, or a sanctuary. A. B. Davidson (Job, 169) and others take the word to mean &quot;judgment seat&quot; or &quot;tribunal&quot; in this context.

1 sn As the book is now arranged, this chapter forms an additional speech by Job, although some argue that it comes from the writer of the book. The mood of the chapter is not despair, but wisdom; it anticipates the divine speeches in the end of the book. This poem, like many psalms in the Bible, has a refrain (vv. 12 and 20). These refrains outline the chapter, giving three sections: there is no known road to wisdom (1-11); no price can buy it (12-19); and only God has it, and only by revelation can man posses it (20-28). 2 tn The poem opens with כִּי (ki). Some commentators think this should have been &quot;for,&quot; and that the poem once stood in another setting. But there are places in the Bible where this word occurs with the sense of &quot;surely&quot; and no other meaning (cf. Gen 18:20). 3 tn The word מוֹצָא (motsa&apos;, from יָצָא [yatsa&apos;, &quot;go out&quot;]) is the word for &quot;mine,&quot; or more simply, &quot;source.&quot; Mining was not an enormous industry in the land of Canaan or Israel; mined products were imported. Some editors have suggested alternative readings: Dahood found in the word the root for &quot;shine&quot; and translated the MT as &quot;smelter.&quot; But that is going too far. P. Joüon suggested &quot;place of finding,&quot; reading מִמְצָא (mimtsa&apos;) for מוֹצָא (motsa&apos;; see Bib 11 [1930]: 323). 4 tn The verb יָזֹקּוּ (yazoqqu) translated &quot;refined,&quot; comes from זָקַק (zaqaq), a word that basically means &quot;to blow.&quot; From the meaning &quot;to blow; to distend; to inflate&quot; derives the meaning for refining.

5 tn Heb &quot;from dust.&quot; 6 tn The verb יָצוּק (yatsuq) is usually translated as a passive participle &quot;is smelted&quot; (from יָצַק [yatsaq, &quot;to melt&quot;]): &quot;copper is smelted from the ore&quot; (ESV) or &quot;from the stone, copper is poured out&quot; (as an imperfect from צוּק [tsuq]). But the rock becomes the metal in the process. So according to R. Gordis (Job, 304) the translation should be: &quot;the rock is poured out as copper.&quot; E. Dhorme (Job, 400), however, defines the form in the text as &quot;hard,&quot; and simply has it &quot;hard stone becomes copper.&quot;

7 sn The text appears at first to be saying that by opening up a mine shaft, or by taking lights down below, the miner dispels the darkness. But the clause might be more general, meaning that man goes deep into the earth as if it were day. 8 tn The verse ends with &quot;the stone of darkness and deep darkness.&quot; The genitive would be location, describing the place where the stones are found.

1 sn There are now four speeches from another friend of Job, Elihu. But Job does not reply to any of these, nor does the Lord. The speeches show a knowledge of the debate that has gone on, but they take a different approach entirely. Elihu&apos;s approach is that suffering is a discipline from God, to teach his people. In other words, Job was suffering to vindicate God&apos;s confidence in him. His speeches are an interesting part of the book, but they too are irrelevant to Job&apos;s actual case. In the first speech, there is a short introduction (32:1-5), and then the speech proper with these sections: Elihu will speak because his youth is wiser (32:6-14), and his friends arguments failed (32:15-22); he calls for Job&apos;s attention (33:1-7), claims Job&apos;s case is wrong (33:8-13), and Job&apos;s argument that God does not answer is false (33:14-28), and then makes an appeal to Job (33:29-33). It becomes evident that Elihu correctly identified Job&apos;s determination to maintain his integrity at God&apos;s expense as the primary problem in at least the latter stages of the dialogues (32:1-3; 34:37; 35:16; cf. 38:2; 40:8; 42:3). Elihu was respectful of his elders (32:4), but remained uninfected by their error (32:14). He sought to maintain impartiality (32:21-22) and to offer true wisdom (33:33), believed like Job that a mediator existed (33:23-24), and desired Job&apos;s vindication (33:32). In addition, Elihu focused on vindicating God&apos;s actions (34:12; 35:10-11; 36:2-3, 22-26) and announced the coming theophany (37:1-5, 22). It appears that he was not included in the divine condemnation of Job&apos;s friends (42:7-9) and was excluded from Job&apos;s prayer of intercession (42:8-10) - both perhaps implying divine approval of his behavior and words. 2 tn The form is the infinitive construct (&quot;answer&quot;) functioning as the object of the preposition; the phrase forms the complement of the verb &quot;they ceased to answer&quot; (= &quot;they refused to answer further&quot;). 3 tc The LXX, Syriac, and Symmachus have &quot;in their eyes.&quot; This is adopted by some commentators, but it does not fit the argument.

4 tn The verse begins with וַיִּחַר אַף (vayyikhar &apos;af, &quot;and the anger became hot&quot;), meaning Elihu became very angry. 5 tn The second comment about Elihu&apos;s anger comes right before the statement of its cause. Now the perfect verb is used: &quot;he was angry.&quot; 6 tn The explanation is the causal clause עַל־צַדְּקוֹ נַפְשׁוֹ (&apos;al-tsaddÿqo nafsho, &quot;because he justified himself&quot;). It is the preposition with the Piel infinitive construct with a suffixed subjective genitive. 7 tc The LXX and Latin versions soften the expression slightly by saying &quot;before God.&quot;

8 tn Heb &quot;his&quot;; the referent (Job) has been specified in the translation to indicate whose friends they were. 9 tn The perfect verb should be given the category of potential perfect here. 10 tc This is one of the eighteen &quot;corrections of the scribes&quot; (tiqqune sopherim); it originally read, &quot;and they declared God [in the wrong].&quot; The thought was that in abandoning the debate they had conceded Job&apos;s point.

1 sn This is the culmination of it all, the revelation of the Lord to Job. Most interpreters see here the style and content of the author of the book, a return to the beginning of the book. Here the Lord speaks to Job and displays his sovereign power and glory. Job has lived through the suffering - without cursing God. He has held to his integrity, and nowhere regretted it. But he was unaware of the real reason for the suffering, and will remain unaware throughout these speeches. God intervenes to resolve the spiritual issues that surfaced. Job was not punished for sin. And Job&apos;s suffering had not cut him off from God. In the end the point is that Job cannot have the knowledge to make the assessments he made. It is wiser to bow in submission and adoration of God than to try to judge him. The first speech of God has these sections: the challenge (38:1-3), the surpassing mysteries of earth and sky beyond Job&apos;s understanding (4-38), and the mysteries of animal and bird life that surpassed his understanding (38:39-39:30). 2 sn This is not the storm described by Elihu - in fact, the Lord ignores Elihu. The storm is a common accompaniment for a theophany (see Ezek 1:4; Nah 1:3; Zech 9:14).

3 tn The demonstrative pronoun is used here to emphasize the interrogative pronoun (see GKC 442 §136.c). 4 sn The referent of &quot;counsel&quot; here is not the debate between Job and the friends, but the purposes of God (see Ps 33:10; Prov 19:21; Isa 19:17). Dhorme translates it &quot;Providence.&quot;

5 tn Heb &quot;Gird up your loins.&quot; This idiom basically describes taking the hem of the long garment or robe and pulling it up between the legs and tucking it into the front of the belt, allowing easier and freer movement of the legs. &quot;Girding the loins&quot; meant the preparation for some difficult task (Jer 1:17), or for battle (Isa 5:27), or for running (1 Kgs 18:46). C. Gordon suggests that it includes belt-wrestling, a form of hand-to-hand mortal combat (&quot;Belt-wrestling in the Bible World,&quot; HUCA 23 [1950/51]: 136).

1 tn The expression &quot;you asked&quot; is added here to clarify the presence of the line to follow. Many commentators delete it as a gloss from Job 38:2. If it is retained, then Job has to be recalling God&apos;s question before he answers it. 2 tn The word לָכֵן (lakhen) is simply &quot;but,&quot; as in Job 31:37. 3 tn Heb &quot;and I do not understand.&quot; The expression serves here in an adverbial capacity. It also could be subordinated as a complement: &quot;I have declared [things that] I do not understand.&quot; 4 tn The last clause is &quot;and I do not know.&quot; This is also subordinated to become a dependent clause.

172.content: 1 sn See N. C. Habel, &quot;The Narrative Art of Job,&quot; JSOT 27 (1983): 101-11; J. J. Owens, &quot;Prologue and Epilogue,&quot; RevExp 68 (1971): 457-67; and R. Polzin, &quot;The Framework of the Book of Job,&quot; Int 31 (1974): 182-200. 2 sn The Book of Job is one of the major books of wisdom literature in the Bible. But it is a different kind of wisdom. Whereas the Book of Proverbs is a collection of the short wisdom sayings, Job is a thorough analysis of the relationship between suffering and divine justice put in a dramatic poetic form. There are a number of treatises on this subject in the ancient Near East, but none of them are as thorough and masterful as Job. See J. Gray, &quot;The Book of Job in the Context of Near Eastern Literature,&quot; ZAW 82 (1970): 251-69; S. N. Kramer, &quot;Man and His God, A Sumerian Variation on the &apos;Job&apos; Motif,&quot; VTSup 3 (1953): 170-82. While the book has fascinated readers for ages, it is a difficult book, difficult to translate and difficult to study. Most of it is written in poetic parallelism. But it is often very cryptic, it is written with unusual grammatical constructions, and it makes use of a large number of very rare words. All this has led some scholars to question if it was originally written in Hebrew or some other related Semitic dialect or language first. There is no indication of who the author was. It is even possible that the work may have been refined over the years; but there is no evidence for this either. The book uses a variety of genres (laments, hymns, proverbs, and oracles) in the various speeches of the participants. This all adds to the richness of the material. And while it is a poetic drama using cycles of speeches, there is no reason to doubt that the events represented here do not go back to a real situation and preserve the various arguments. Several indications in the book would place Job&apos;s dates in the time of the patriarchs. But the composition of the book, or at least its final form, may very well come from the first millennium, maybe in the time of the flowering of wisdom literature with Solomon. We have no way of knowing when the book was written, or when its revision was completed. But dating it late in the intertestamental period is ruled out by the appearance of translations and copies of it, notably bits of a Targum of Job in the Dead Sea Scrolls. Among the general works and commentaries, see A. Hurvitz, &quot;The Date of the Prose Tale of Job Linguistically Reconsidered,&quot; HTR 67 (1974): 17-34; R. H. Pfeiffer, &quot;The Priority of Job over Isaiah 40-55,&quot; JBL 46 (1927): 202ff. The book presents many valuable ideas on the subject of the suffering of the righteous. Ultimately it teaches that one must submit to the wisdom of the Creator. But it also indicates that the shallow answers of Job&apos;s friends do not do justice to the issue. Their arguments that suffering is due to sin are true to a point, but they did not apply to Job. His protests sound angry and belligerent, but he held tenaciously to his integrity. His experience shows that it is possible to live a pure life and yet still suffer. He finally turns his plea to God, demanding a hearing. This he receives, of course, only to hear that God is sovereignly ruling the universe. Job can only submit to him. In the end God does not abandon his sufferer. For additional material, see G. L. Archer, The Book of Job; H. H. Rowley, &quot;The Book of Job and Its Meaning,&quot; BJRL 41 (1958/59): 167-207; J. A. Baker, The Book of Job; C. L. Feinberg, &quot;The Book of Job,&quot; BSac 91 (1934): 78-86; R. Polzin and D. Robertson, &quot;Studies in the Book of Job,&quot; Semeia 7 (Missoula: Scholars Press, 1977). 3 tn The Hebrew construction is literally &quot;a man was,&quot; using אִישׁ הָיָה (&apos;ish hayah) rather than a preterite first. This simply begins the narrative. 4 sn The term Uz occurs several times in the Bible: a son of Aram (Gen 10:23), a son of Nahor (Gen 22:21), and a descendant of Seir (Gen 36:28). If these are the clues to follow, the location would be north of Syria or south near Edom. The book tells how Job&apos;s flocks were exposed to Chaldeans, the tribes between Syria and the Euphrates (1:17), and in another direction to attacks from the Sabeans (1:15). The most prominent man among his friends was from Teman, which was in Edom (2:11). Uz is also connected with Edom in Lamentations 4:21. The most plausible location, then, would be east of Israel and northeast of Edom, in what is now North Arabia. The LXX has &quot;on the borders of Edom and Arabia.&quot; An early Christian tradition placed his home in an area about 40 miles south of Damascus, in Baashan at the southeast foot of Hermon. 5 tn In Hebrew the defining relative clause (&quot;whose name was Job&quot;) is actually an asyndetic verbless noun-clause placed in apposition to the substantive (&quot;a man&quot;); see GKC 486 §155.e. 6 sn The name &quot;Job&quot; is mentioned by Ezekiel as one of the greats in the past - Noah, Job, and Daniel (14:14). The suffering of Job was probably well known in the ancient world, and this name was clearly part of that tradition. There is little reason to try to determine the etymology and meaning of the name, since it may not be Hebrew. If it were Hebrew, it might mean something like &quot;persecuted,&quot; although some suggest &quot;aggressor.&quot; If Arabic it might have the significance of &quot;the one who always returns to God.&quot; 7 tn The word תָּם (tam) has been translated &quot;perfect&quot; (so KJV, ASV). The verbal root תָּמַם (tamam) means &quot;to be blameless, complete.&quot; The word is found in Gen 25:27 where it describes Jacob as &quot;even-tempered.&quot; It also occurs in Ps 64:5 (64:4 ET) and Prov 29:10. The meaning is that a person or a thing is complete, perfect, flawless. It does not mean that he was sinless, but that he was wholeheartedly trying to please God, that he had integrity and was blameless before God. 8 tn The word יָשָׁר (yashar, &quot;upright&quot;) is complementary to &quot;blameless.&quot; The idea is &quot;upright, just,&quot; and applies to his relationships with others (Ps 37:37 and 25:21). 9 sn These two expressions indicate the outcome of Job&apos;s character. &quot;Fearing God&quot; and &quot;turning from evil&quot; also express two correlative ideas in scripture; they signify his true piety - he had reverential fear of the Lord, meaning he was a truly devoted worshiper who shunned evil.

10 sn The numbers used in the chapter, seven, three, and five, carry the symbolism in the Bible of perfection and completeness (see J. J. Davis, Biblical Numerology). Job&apos;s &quot;seven sons&quot; are listed first because in the East sons were considered more valuable than daughters (recall Ruth, who is &quot;better than seven sons&quot; [Ruth 4:15]). 11 tn The verb begins the sentence: &quot;and there were born.&quot; This use of the preterite with vav (ו) consecutive, especially after the verb הָיָה (hayah, &quot;to be&quot;), is explanatory: there was a man...and there was born to him...&quot; (IBHS 551-52 §33.2.2b).

12 tn The word means &quot;cattle, livestock, possessions&quot; (see also Gen 26:14). Here it includes the livestock, but also the entire substance of his household. 13 tn Or &quot;amounted to,&quot; &quot;totaled.&quot; The preterite of הָיָה (hayah, &quot;to be&quot;) is sometimes employed to introduce a total amount or an inventory (see Exod 1:5; Num 3:43). 14 tn The word עֲבֻדָּה (&apos;avuddah, &quot;service of household servants&quot;) indicates that he had a very large body of servants, meaning a very large household. 15 tn Heb &quot;and that man.&quot; 16 tn The expression is literally &quot;sons of the east.&quot; The use of the genitive after &quot;sons&quot; in this construction may emphasize their nature (like &quot;sons of belial&quot;); it would refer to them as easterners (like &quot;sons of the south&quot; in contemporary American English). BDB 869 s.v. קֶדֶם says &quot;dwellers in the east.&quot;

17 tn The perfect verb with the ו (vav), וְהָלְכוּ (vÿhalÿkhu, &quot;they went&quot;) indicates their characteristic action, actions that were frequently repeated (GKC 335-36 §112.dd). 18 tn Heb &quot;make a feast.&quot; 19 tn The sense is cryptic; it literally says &quot;house - a man - his day.&quot; The word &quot;house&quot; is an adverbial accusative of place: &quot;in the house.&quot; &quot;Man&quot; is the genitive; it also has a distributive sense: &quot;in the house of each man.&quot; And &quot;his day&quot; is an adverbial accusative: &quot;on his day.&quot; The point is that they feasted every day of the week in rotation. 20 tn The use of קָרָא (qara&apos;, &quot;to call, invite&quot;) followed by the ל (lamed) usually has the force of &quot;to summon.&quot; Here the meaning would not be so commanding, but would refer to an invitation (see also 1 Kgs 1:19, 25, 26). 21 tn Normally cardinal numerals tend to disagree in gender with the numbered noun. In v. 2 &quot;three daughters&quot; consists of the masculine numeral followed by the feminine noun. However, here &quot;three sisters&quot; consists of the feminine numeral followed by the feminine noun. The distinction appears to be that the normal disagreement between numeral and noun when the intent is merely to fix the number (3 daughters as opposed to 2 or 4 daughters). However, when a particular, previously known group is indicated, the numeral tends to agree with the noun in gender. A similar case occurs in Gen 3:13 (&quot;three wives&quot; of Noah&apos;s sons).

22 tn The verse begins with the temporal indicator &quot;and it happened&quot; or &quot;and it came to pass,&quot; which need not be translated. The particle כִּי (ki, &quot;when&quot;) with the initial verbal form indicates it is a temporal clause. 23 tn The verb is the Hiphil perfect of נָקַף (naqaf, &quot;go around&quot;), here it means &quot;to make the round&quot; or &quot;complete the circuit&quot; (BDB 668-69 s.v. II נָקַף Hiph). It indicates that when the feasting had made its circuit of the seven sons, then Job would sanctify them. 24 tn The form is a preterite with vav (ו) consecutive. The same emphasis on repeated or frequent action continues here in this verse. The idea here is that Job would send for them, because the sanctification of them would have consisted of washings and changes of garments as well as the sacrifices (see Gen 35:2; 1 Sam 16:5). 25 tn Or &quot;purify.&quot; 26 tn The first verb could also be joined with the next to form a verbal hendiadys: &quot;he would rise early and he would sacrifice&quot; would then simply be &quot;he would sacrifice early in the morning&quot; (see M. Delcor, &quot;Quelques cas de survivances du vocabulaire nomade en hébreu biblique,&quot; VT 25 [1975]: 307-22). This section serves to explain in more detail how Job sanctified his children. sn In the patriarchal society it was normal for the father to act as priest for the family, making the sacrifices as needed. Job here is exceptional in his devotion to the duty. The passage shows the balance between the greatest earthly rejoicing by the family, and the deepest piety and affection of the father. 27 tn The text does not have &quot;according to&quot;; the noun &quot;number&quot; is an accusative that defines the extent of his actions (GKC 373-74 §118.e, h). 28 tn The clause stands as an accusative to the verb, here as the direct object introduced with &quot;perhaps&quot; (IBHS 645-46 §38.8d). 29 tn Heb &quot;sons,&quot; but since the three daughters are specifically mentioned in v. 4, &quot;children&quot; has been used in the translation. In this patriarchal culture, however, it is possible that only the sons are in view. 30 tn The Hebrew verb is בָּרַךְ (barakh), which means &quot;to bless.&quot; Here is a case where the writer or a scribe has substituted the word &quot;curse&quot; with the word &quot;bless&quot; to avoid having the expression &quot;curse God.&quot; For similar euphemisms in the ancient world, see K. A. Kitchen, Ancient Orient and Old Testament, 166. It is therefore difficult to know exactly what Job feared they might have done. The opposite of &quot;bless&quot; would be &quot;curse,&quot; which normally would convey disowning or removing from blessing. Some commentators try to offer a definition of &quot;curse&quot; from the root in the text, and noting that &quot;curse&quot; is too strong, come to something like &quot;renounce.&quot; The idea of blaspheming is probably not meant; rather, in their festivities they may have said things that renounced God or their interest in him. Job feared this momentary turning away from God in their festivities, perhaps as they thought their good life was more important than their religion. 31 tn The imperfect expresses continual action in past time, i.e., a customary imperfect (GKC 315 §107.e).

32 sn The text draws the curtain of heaven aside for the reader to understand the background of this drama. God extols the virtue of Job, but Satan challenges the reasons for it. He receives permission to try to dislodge Job from his integrity. In short, God is using Job to prove Satan&apos;s theory wrong. 33 tn The beginning Hebrew expression &quot;and there was - the day&quot; indicates that &quot;there came a day when&quot; or more simply &quot;the day came when.&quot; It emphasizes the particular day. The succeeding clause is then introduced with a preterite with the with vav (ו) consecutive (see E. Dhorme, Job, 5). 34 sn The &quot;sons of God&quot; in the OT is generally taken to refer to angels. They are not actually &quot;sons&quot; of Elohim; the idiom is a poetic way of describing their nature and relationship to God. The phrase indicates their supernatural nature, and their submission to God as the sovereign Lord. It may be classified as a genitive that expresses how individuals belong to a certain class or type, i.e., the supernatural (GKC 418 §128.v). In the pagan literature, especially of Ugarit, &quot;the sons of God&quot; refers to the lesser gods or deities of the pantheon. See H. W. Robinson, &quot;The Council of Yahweh,&quot; JTS 45 (1943): 151-57; G. Cooke, &quot;The Sons of (the) God(s),&quot; ZAW 76 (1964): 22-47; M. Tsevat, &quot;God and the Gods in the Assembly,&quot; HUCA 40-41 (1969/70): 123-37. 35 tn The preposition עַל (&apos;al) in this construction after a verb of standing or going means &quot;before&quot; (GKC 383 §119.cc). 36 sn The word means &quot;adversary&quot; or with the article &quot;the adversary&quot; - here the superhuman adversary or Satan. The word with the article means that the meaning of the word should receive prominence. A denominative verb meaning &quot;to act as adversary&quot; occurs. Satan is the great accuser of the saints (see Zech 3 where &quot;Satan was standing there to &apos;satanize&apos; Joshua the priest&quot;; and see Rev 12 which identifies him with the Serpent in Genesis). He came among the angels at this time because he is one of them and has access among them. Even though fallen, Satan has yet to be cast down completely (see Rev 12).

37 tn The imperfect may be classified as progressive imperfect; it indicates action that although just completed is regarded as still lasting into the present (GKC 316 §107.h). 38 tn Heb &quot;answered the Lord and said&quot; (also in v. 9). The words &quot;and said&quot; here and in v. 9 have not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons. 39 tn The verb שׁוּט (shut) means &quot;to go or rove about&quot; (BDB 1001-2 s.v.). Here the infinitive construct serves as the object of the preposition. 40 tn The Hitpael (here also an infinitive construct after the preposition) of the verb הָלַךְ (halakh) means &quot;to walk to and fro, back and forth, with the sense of investigating or reconnoitering (see e.g. Gen 13:17). sn As the words are spoken by Satan, there is no self-condemnation in them. What they signify is the swiftness and thoroughness of his investigation of humans. The good angels are said to go to and fro in the earth on behalf of the suffering righteous (Zech 1:10, 11; 6:7), but Satan goes seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet 5:8).

41 tn The Hebrew has &quot;have you placed your heart on Job?&quot; This means &quot;direct your mind to&quot; (cf. BDB 963 s.v. I שׂוּם 2.b). sn The question is undoubtedly rhetorical, for it is designed to make Satan aware of Job as God extols his fine qualities. 42 tn The Hebrew conjunction כִּי (ki) need not be translated in this case or it might be taken as emphatic (cf. IBHS 665 §39.3.4e): &quot;Certainly there is no one like him.&quot; 43 tn The same expressions that appeared at the beginning of the chapter appear here in the words of God. In contrast to that narrative report about Job, the emphasis here is on Job&apos;s present character, and so the participle form is translated here asa gnomic or characteristic present (&quot;turns&quot;). It modifies &quot;man&quot; as one who is turning from evil.

44 tn The Hebrew form has the interrogative ה (he) on the adverb חִנָּם (khinnam, &quot;gratis&quot;), a derivative either of the verb חָנַן (khanan, &quot;to be gracious, show favor&quot;), or its related noun חֵן (khen, &quot;grace, favor&quot;). The adverb has the sense of &quot;free; gratis; gratuitously; for nothing; for no reason&quot; (see BDB 336 s.v. חִנָּם). The idea is that Satan does not disagree that Job is pious, but that Job is loyal to God because of what he receives from God. He will test the sincerity of Job.

45 tn The use of the independent personal pronoun here emphasizes the subject of the verb: &quot;Have you not put up a hedge.&quot; 46 tn The verb שׂוּךְ (sukh) means &quot;to hedge or fence up, about&quot; something (BDB 962 s.v. I שׂוּךְ). The original idea seems to have been to surround with a wall of thorns for the purpose of protection (E. Dhorme, Job, 7). The verb is an implied comparison between making a hedge and protecting someone. 47 sn Here the verb &quot;bless&quot; is used in one of its very common meanings. The verb means &quot;to enrich,&quot; often with the sense of enabling or empowering things for growth or fruitfulness. See further C. Westermann, Blessing in the Bible and the Life of the Church (OBT). 48 tn Or &quot;substance.&quot; The herds of livestock may be taken by metonymy of part for whole to represent possessions or prosperity in general. 49 tn The verb פָּרַץ (parats) means &quot;to break through.&quot; It has the sense of abundant increase, as in breaking out, overflowing (see also Gen 30:30 and Exod 1:12).

50 tn The particle אוּלָם (&apos;ulam, &quot;but&quot;) serves to restrict the clause in relation to the preceding clause (IBHS 671-73 §39.3.5e, n. 107). 51 tn The force of the imperatives in this sentence are almost conditional - if God were to do this, then surely Job would respond differently. sn The two imperatives (&quot;stretch out&quot; and &quot;strike&quot;) and the word &quot;hand&quot; all form a bold anthropomorphic sentence. It is as if God would deliver a blow to Job with his fist. But the intended meaning is that God would intervene to destroy Job&apos;s material and physical prosperity. 52 sn The formula used in the expression is the oath formula: &quot;if not to your face he will curse you&quot; meaning &quot;he will surely curse you to your face.&quot; Satan is so sure that the piety is insincere that he can use an oath formula. 53 tn See the comments on Job 1:5. Here too the idea of &quot;renounce&quot; may fit well enough; but the idea of actually cursing God may not be out of the picture if everything Job has is removed. Satan thinks he will denounce God.

54 tn The particle הִנֵּה (hinneh, &quot;behold&quot;) introduces a foundational clause upon which the following volitional clause is based. 55 tn The versions add a verb here: &quot;delivered to&quot; or &quot;abandoned to&quot; the hand of Satan. 56 tn Heb &quot;in your hand.&quot; The idiom means that it is now Satan&apos;s to do with as he pleases. 57 tn The Hebrew word order emphatically holds out Job&apos;s person as the exception: &quot;only upon him do not stretch forth your hand.&quot; 58 tn The Targum to Job adds &quot;with permission&quot; to show that he was granted leave from God&apos;s presence. 59 sn So Satan, having received his permission to test Job&apos;s sincerity, goes out from the Lord&apos;s presence. But Satan is bound by the will of the Most High not to touch Job himself. The sentence gives the impression that Satan&apos;s departure is with a certain eagerness and confidence.

60 sn The series of catastrophes and the piety of Job is displayed now in comprehensive terms. Everything that can go wrong goes wrong, and yet Job, the pious servant of Yahweh, continues to worship him in the midst of the rubble. This section, and the next, will lay the foundation for the great dialogues in the book. 61 tn The Targum to Job clarifies that it was the first day of the week. The fact that it was in the house of the firstborn is the reason. 62 tn Heb &quot;his&quot;; the referent (Job) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
63 tn The use of the verb &quot;to be&quot; with the participle gives emphasis to the continuing of the action in the past (GKC 360 §116.r).

64 tn The LXX has &quot;the spoilers spoiled them&quot; instead of &quot;the Sabeans swooped down.&quot; The translators might have connected the word to שְָׁבָה (shavah, &quot;to take captive&quot;) rather than שְׁבָא (shÿva&apos;, &quot;Sabeans&quot;), or they may have understood the name as general reference to all types of Bedouin invaders from southern Arabia (HALOT 1381 s.v. שְׁבָא 2.c). sn The name &quot;Sheba&quot; is used to represent its inhabitants, or some of them. The verb is feminine because the name is a place name. The Sabeans were a tribe from the Arabian peninsula. They were traders mostly (6:19). The raid came from the south, suggesting that this band of Sabeans were near Edom. The time of the attack seems to be winter since the oxen were plowing. 65 tn The Hebrew is simply &quot;fell&quot; (from נָפַל, nafal). To &quot;fall upon&quot; something in war means to attack quickly and suddenly. 66 sn Job&apos;s servants were probably armed and gave resistance, which would be the normal case in that time. This was probably why they were &quot;killed with the sword.&quot; 67 tn Heb &quot;the edge/mouth of the sword&quot;; see T. J. Meek, &quot;Archaeology and a Point of Hebrew Syntax,&quot; BASOR 122 (1951): 31-33. 68 tn The pleonasms in the verse emphasize the emotional excitement of the messenger.

69 tn The particle עוֹד (&apos;od, &quot;still&quot;) is used with the participle to express the past circumstances when something else happened (IBHS 625-26 §37.6d). 70 tn The Hebrew expression is literally &quot;yet/this/speaking/and this/ arrived.&quot; The sentence uses the two demonstratives as a contrasting pair. It means &quot;this one was still speaking when that one arrived&quot; (IBHS 308-9 §17.3c). The word &quot;messenger&quot; has been supplied in the translation in vv. 16, 17, and 18 for clarity and for stylistic reasons. 71 sn The &quot;fire of God&quot; would refer to lightning (1 Kgs 18:38; 2 Kgs 1:12; cf. NAB, NCV, TEV). The LXX simply has &quot;fire.&quot; The first blow came from enemies; the second from heaven, which might have confused Job more as to the cause of his troubles. The use of the divine epithet could also be an indication of the superlative degree; see D. W. Thomas, &quot;A Consideration of Some Unusual Ways of Expressing the Superlative in Hebrew,&quot; VT 3 (1953): 209-24. 72 tn Or &quot;from the sky.&quot; The Hebrew word שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated &quot;heaven[s]&quot; or &quot;sky&quot; depending on the context.

73 sn The name may have been given to the tribes that roamed between the Euphrates and the lands east of the Jordan. These are possibly the nomadic Kaldu who are part of the ethnic Aramaeans. The LXX simply has &quot;horsemen.&quot; 74 tn The verb פָּשַׁט (pashat) means &quot;to hurl themselves&quot; upon something (see Judg 9:33, 41). It was a quick, plundering raid to carry off the camels. 75 tn Heb &quot;with the edge/mouth of the sword.&quot;

76 tn The use of the particle הִנֵּה (hinneh, &quot;behold&quot;) in this sentence is deictic, pointing out with excitement the events that happened as if the listener was there. 77 sn Both wind and lightning (v. 16) were employed by Satan as his tools. God can permit him such control over factors of the weather when it suits the divine purpose, but God retains ultimate control (see 28:23-27; Prov 3:4; Luke 8:24-25). 78 tn The word מֵעֵבֶר (me&apos;ever) is simply &quot;from the direction of&quot;; the word עֵבֶר (&apos;ever) indicates the area the whirlwind came across.

79 tn The verb וַיָּקָם (vayyaqom, &quot;and he arose&quot;) indicates the intentionality and the rapidity of the actions to follow. It signals the beginning of his response to the terrible news. Therefore, the sentence could be translated, &quot;Then Job immediately began to tear his robe.&quot; 80 sn It was the custom to tear the robe in a time of mourning, to indicate that the heart was torn (Joel 2:13). The &quot;garment, mantel&quot; here is the outer garment frequently worn over the basic tunic. See further D. R. Ap-Thomas, &quot;Notes on Some Terms Relating to Prayer,&quot; VT 6 (1956): 220-24. 81 sn In mourning one normally put off every adornment that enhanced or embellished the person, including that which nature provided (Jer 7:29; Mic 1:16). 82 tn This last verb is the Hishtaphel of the word חָוָה (khavah; BDB 1005 s.v. שָׁחָה); it means &quot;to prostrate oneself, to cause oneself to be low to the ground.&quot; In the OT it is frequently translated &quot;to worship&quot; because that is usually why the individual would kneel down and then put his or her forehead to the ground at the knees. But the word essentially means &quot;to bow down to the ground.&quot; Here &quot;worship&quot; (although employed by several English translations, cf. KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV, CEV) conveys more than what is taking place - although Job&apos;s response is certainly worshipful. See G. I. Davies, &quot;A Note on the Etymology of histahawah,&quot; VT 29 (1979): 493-95; and J. A. Emerton, &quot;The Etymology of histahawah,&quot; OTS (1977): 41-55.

83 tn The adjective &quot;naked&quot; is functioning here as an adverbial accusative of state, explicative of the state of the subject. While it does include the literal sense of nakedness at birth, Job is also using it symbolically to mean &quot;without possessions.&quot; 84 sn While the first half of the couplet is to be taken literally as referring to his coming into this life, this second part must be interpreted only generally to refer to his departure from this life. It is parallel to 1 Tim 6:7, &quot;For we have brought nothing into this world and so we cannot take a single thing out either.&quot; 85 tn The two verbs are simple perfects. (1) They can be given the nuance of gnomic imperfect, expressing what the sovereign God always does. This is the approach taken in the present translation. Alternatively (2) they could be referring specifically to Job&apos;s own experience: &quot;Yahweh gave [definite past, referring to his coming into this good life] and Yahweh has taken away&quot; [present perfect, referring to his great losses]. Many English versions follow the second alternative. 86 sn Some commentators are troubled by the appearance of the word &quot;Yahweh&quot; on the lips of Job, assuming that the narrator inserted his own name for God into the story-telling. Such thinking is based on the assumption that Yahweh was only a national god of Israel, unknown to anyone else in the ancient world. But here is a clear indication that a non-Israelite, Job, knew and believed in Yahweh.

87 tn The last clause is difficult to translate. It simply reads, &quot;and he did not give unseemliness to God.&quot; The word תִּפְלָה (tiflah) means &quot;unsavoriness&quot; or &quot;unseemliness&quot; in a moral sense. The sense is that Job did not charge God with any moral impropriety in his dealings with him. God did nothing worthless or tasteless. The ancient versions saw the word connected with &quot;foolishness&quot; or &quot;stupidity&quot; (תָּפֵל, tafel, &quot;to be tasteless&quot;). It is possible that &quot;folly&quot; would capture some of what Job meant here. See also M. Dahood, &quot;Hebrew-Ugaritic Lexicography XII,&quot; Bib 55 (1974): 381-93.
1 tc This last purpose clause has been omitted in some Greek versions.

2 tn Heb &quot;answered the Lord and said&quot; (also in v. 4). The words &quot;and said&quot; here and in v. 9 have not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons. 3 tn See the note on this phrase in 1:7.

4 tn The form is the Hiphil participle, &quot;make strong, seize, hold fast.&quot; It is the verbal use here; joined with עֹדֶנּוּ (&apos;odennu, &quot;yet he&quot;) it emphasizes that &quot;he is still holding firmly.&quot; The testing has simply strengthened Job in his integrity. 5 tn This is the same word used to describe Job as &quot;blameless, pure.&quot; Here it carries the idea of &quot;integrity&quot;; Job remained blameless, perfect. 6 tn The vav (ו) with the preterite is used here to express the logical conclusion or consequence of what was stated previously. God is saying that Job has maintained his integrity, so that now it is clear that Satan moved against him groundlessly (GKC 328 §111.l). 7 tn The verb literally means &quot;to swallow&quot;; it forms an implied comparison in the line, indicating the desire of Satan to ruin him completely. See A Guillaume, &quot;A Note on the Root bala`,&quot; JTS 13 (1962): 320-23; and N. M. Sarna, &quot;Epic Substratum in the Prose of Job,&quot;JBL 76 (1957): 13-25, for a discussion of the Ugaritic deity Mot swallowing up the enemy. 8 sn Once again the adverb חִנָּם (khinnam, &quot;gratis&quot;) is used. It means &quot;graciously, gratis, free, without cause, for no reason.&quot; Here the sense has to be gratuitously, for no reason.&quot; The point of the verb חָנַן (khanan, &quot;to be gracious&quot;) and its derivatives is that the action is undeserved. In fact, they would deserve the opposite. Sinners seeking grace deserve punishment. Here, Job deserves reward, not suffering.

1 sn The previous chapters (1-2) were prose narrative, this chapter, however, commences the poetic section of the book (chs. 3-41) containing the cycles of speeches. 2 sn The detailed introduction to the speech with &quot;he opened his mouth&quot; draws the readers attention to what was going to be said. As the introduction to the poetic speech that follows (3:3-26), vv. 1-2 continue the prose style of chapters 1-2. Each of the subsequent speeches is introduced by such a prose heading. 3 tn The verb &quot;cursed&quot; is the Piel preterite from the verb קָלַל (qalal); this means &quot;to be light&quot; in the Qal stem, but here &quot;to treat lightly, with contempt, curse.&quot; See in general H. C. Brichto, The Problem of &quot;Curse&quot; in the Hebrew Bible (JBLMS); and A. C. Thiselton, &quot;The Supposed Power of Words in the Biblical Writings,&quot; JTS 25 (1974): 283-99. 4 tn Heb &quot;his day&quot; (so KJV, ASV, NAB). The Syriac has &quot;the day on which he was born.&quot; The context makes it clear that Job meant the day of his birth. But some have tried to offer a different interpretation, such as his destiny or his predicament. For this reason the Syriac clarified the meaning for their readers in much the same way as the present translation does by rendering &quot;his day&quot; as &quot;the day he was born.&quot; On the Syriac translation of the book of Job, see Heidi M. Szpek, Translation Technique in the Peshitta to Job (SBLDS).

5 tn The text has וַיַּעַן (vayya&apos;an), literally, &quot;and he answered.&quot; The LXX simply has &quot;saying&quot; for the entire verse. The Syriac, Targum, and Greek A have what the MT has. &quot;[Someone] answered and said&quot; is phraseology characteristic of all the speeches in Job beginning with Satan in 1:9. Only in 40:1 is it employed when God is speaking. No other portion of the OT employs this phraseology as often or as consistently.

6 tn The relative clause is carried by the preposition with the resumptive pronoun: &quot;the day [which] I was born in it&quot; meaning &quot;the day on which I was born&quot; (see GKC 486-88 §155.f, i). 7 tn The verb is the Niphal imperfect. It may be interpreted in this dependent clause (1) as representing a future event from some point of time in the past - &quot;the day on which I was born&quot; or &quot;would be born&quot; (see GKC 316 §107.k). Or (2) it may simply serve as a preterite indicating action that is in the past. 8 tn The MT simply has &quot;and the night - it said....&quot; By simple juxtaposition with the parallel construction (&quot;on which I was born&quot;) the verb &quot;it said&quot; must be a relative clause explaining &quot;the night.&quot; Rather than supply &quot;in which&quot; and make the verb passive (which is possible since no specific subject is provided, but leaves open the question of who said it), it is preferable to take the verse as a personification. First Job cursed the day; now he cursed the night that spoke about what it witnessed. See A. Ehrman, &quot;A Note on the Verb &apos;amar,&quot; JQR 55 (1964/65): 166-67. 9 tn The word is גֶּבֶר (gever, &quot;a man&quot;). The word usually distinguishes a man as strong, distinct from children and women. Translations which render this as &quot;boy&quot; (to remove the apparent contradiction of an adult being &quot;conceived&quot; in the womb) miss this point. 10 sn The announcement at birth is to the fact that a male was conceived. The same parallelism between &quot;brought forth/born&quot; and &quot;conceived&quot; may be found in Ps 51:7 HT (51:5 ET). The motifs of the night of conception and the day of birth will be developed by Job. For the entire verse, which is more a wish or malediction than a curse, see S. H. Blank, &quot;&apos;Perish the Day!&apos; A Misdirected Curse (Job 3:3),&quot; Prophetic Thought, 61-63.

1 sn The speech of Eliphaz can be broken down into three main sections. In 4:1-11 he wonders that Job who had comforted so many people in trouble, and who was so pious, should fall into such despair, forgetting the great truth that the righteous never perish under affliction - calamity only destroys the wicked. Then in 4:12-5:7 Eliphaz tries to warn Job about complaining against God because only the ungodly resent the dealings of God and by their impatience bring down his wrath upon them. Finally in 5:8-27 Eliphaz appeals to Job to follow a different course, to seek after God, for God only smites to heal or to correct, to draw people to himself and away from evil. See K. Fullerton, &quot;Double Entendre in the First Speech of Eliphaz,&quot; JBL 49 (1930): 320-74; J. C. L. Gibson, &quot;Eliphaz the Temanite: A Portrait of a Hebrew Philosopher,&quot; SJT 28 (1975): 259-72; and J. Lust, &quot;A Stormy Vision: Some Remarks on Job 4:12-16,&quot; Bijdr 36 (1975): 308-11. 2 tn Heb &quot;answered and said.&quot;

3 tn The verb has no expressed subject, and so may be translated with &quot;one&quot; or &quot;someone.&quot; 4 tn The Piel perfect is difficult here. It would normally be translated &quot;has one tried (words with you)?&quot; Most commentaries posit a conditional clause, however. 5 tn The verb means &quot;to be weary.&quot; But it can have the extended sense of being either exhausted or impatient (see v. 5). A. B. Davidson (Job, 29) takes it in the sense of &quot;will it be too much for you?&quot; There is nothing in the sentence that indicates this should be an interrogative clause; it is simply an imperfect. But in view of the juxtaposition of the first part, this seems to make good sense. E. Dhorme (Job, 42) has &quot;Shall we address you? You are dejected.&quot; 6 tn The construction uses a noun with the preposition: &quot;and to refrain with words - who is able?&quot; The Aramaic plural of &quot;words&quot; (מִלִּין, millin) occurs 13 times in Job, with the Hebrew plural ten times. The commentaries show that Eliphaz&apos;s speech had a distinctly Aramaic coloring to it.

7 tn The deictic particle הִנֵּה (hinneh, &quot;behold&quot;) summons attention; it has the sense of &quot;consider, look.&quot; 8 tn The verb יָסַר (yasar) in the Piel means &quot;to correct,&quot; whether by words with the sense of teach, or by chastening with the sense of punish, discipline. The double meaning of &quot;teach&quot; and &quot;discipline&quot; is also found with the noun מוּסָר (musar). 9 tn The parallelism again uses a perfect verb in the first colon and an imperfect in the second; but since the sense of the line is clearly what Job has done in the past, the second verb may be treated as a preterite, or a customary imperfect - what Job repeatedly did in the past (GKC 315 §107.e). The words in this verse may have double meanings. The word יָסַר (yasar, &quot;teach, discipline&quot;) may have the idea of instruction and correction, but also the connotation of strength (see Y. Hoffmann, &quot;The Use of Equivocal Words in the First Speech of Eliphaz [Job IV-V],&quot; VT 30 [1980]: 114-19). 10 tn The &quot;feeble hands&quot; are literally &quot;hands hanging down.&quot; This is a sign of weakness, helplessness, or despondency (see 2 Sam 4:1; Isa 13:7).

1 tn Some commentators transpose this verse with the following paragraph, placing it after v. 7 (see E. Dhorme, Job, 62). But the reasons for this are based on the perceived development of the argument and are not that compelling. sn The imperative is here a challenge for Job. If he makes his appeal against God, who is there who will listen? The rhetorical questions are intended to indicate that no one will respond, not even the angels. Job would do better to realize that he is guilty and his only hope is in God. 2 tn The participle with the suffix could be given a more immediate translation to accompany the imperative: &quot;Call now! Is anyone listening to you?&quot; 3 tn The LXX has rendered &quot;holy ones&quot; as &quot;holy angels&quot; (cf. TEV, CEV, NLT). The LXX has interpreted the verb in the colon too freely: &quot;if you will see.&quot; 4 sn The point being made is that the angels do not represent the cries of people to God as if mediating for them. But if Job appealed to any of them to take his case against God, there would be no response whatsoever for that.

5 tn One of the reasons that commentators transpose v. 1 is that the כִּי (ki, &quot;for&quot;) here seems to follow 4:21 better. If people die without wisdom, it is folly that kills them. But the verse also makes sense after 5:1. He is saying that complaining against God will not bring deliverance (v. 1), but rather, by such impatience the fool will bring greater calamity on himself. 6 tn The two words for &quot;foolish person&quot; are common in wisdom literature. The first, אֱוִיל (&apos;evil), is the fool who is a senseless person; the פֹּתֶה (poteh) is the naive and silly person, the simpleton, the one who is easily led astray. The direct object is introduced with the preposition ל (lamed) in this verse (see GKC 366 §117.n). 7 tn The two parallel nouns are similar; their related verbs are also paralleled in Deut 32:16 with the idea of &quot;vex&quot; and &quot;irritate.&quot; The first word כַּעַשׂ (ka&apos;as) refers to the inner irritation and anger one feels, whereas the second word קִנְאָה (qin&apos;ah) refers to the outward expression of the anger. In Job 6:2, Job will respond &quot;O that my impatience [ka&apos;as] were weighed....&quot;

8 tn The use of the pronoun here adds emphasis to the subject of the sentence (see GKC 437 §135.a). 9 tn This word is אֱוִיל (&apos;evil), the same word for the &quot;senseless man&quot; in the preceding verse. Eliphaz is citing an example of his principle just given - he saw such a fool for a brief while appearing to prosper (i.e., taking root). 10 tn A. B. Davidson argues that the verse does not mean that Eliphaz cursed his place during his prosperity. This line is metonymical (giving the effect). God judged the fool and his place was ruined; consequently, Eliphaz pronounced it accursed of God (see A. B. Davidson, Job, 36). Many emend the verb slightly to read &quot;and it was suddenly cursed&quot; (וַיֻּכַב [vayyukhav] instead of וָאֶקּוֹב [va&apos;eqqov]; see H. H. Rowley, Job [NCBC], 51).

2 tn The conjunction לוּ (lu, &quot;if, if only&quot;) introduces the wish - an unrealizable wish - with the Niphal imperfect. 3 tn Job pairs כַּעְסִי (ka&apos;si, &quot;my grief&quot;) and הַיָּתִי (hayyati, &quot;my misfortune&quot;). The first word, used in Job 4:2, refers to Job&apos;s whole demeanor that he shows his friends - the impatient and vexed expression of his grief. The second word expresses his misfortune, the cause of his grief. Job wants these placed together in the balances so that his friends could see the misfortune is greater than the grief. The word for &quot;misfortune&quot; is a Kethib-Qere reading. The two words have essentially the same meaning; they derive from the verb הָוַה (havah, &quot;to fall&quot;) and so mean a misfortune. 4 tn The Qal infinitive absolute is here used to intensify the Niphal imperfect (see GKC 344-45 §113.w). The infinitive absolute intensifies the wish as well as the idea of weighing. 5 tn The third person plural verb is used here; it expresses an indefinite subject and is treated as a passive (see GKC 460 §144.g). 6 tn The adverb normally means &quot;together,&quot; but it can also mean &quot;similarly, too.&quot; In this verse it may not mean that the two things are to be weighed together, but that the whole calamity should be put on the scales (see A. B. Davidson, Job, 43).

7 tn E. Dhorme (Job, 76) notes that כִּי־עַתָּה (ki &apos;attah) has no more force than &quot;but&quot;; and that the construction is the same as in 17:4; 20:19-21; 23:14-15. The initial clause is causative, and the second half of the verse gives the consequence (&quot;because&quot;...&quot;that is why&quot;). Others take 3a as the apodosis of v. 2, and translate it &quot;for now it would be heavier...&quot; (see A. B. Davidson, Job, 43). 8 sn The point of the comparison with the sand of the sea is that the sand is immeasurable. So the grief of Job cannot be measured. 9 tn The verb לָעוּ (la&apos;u) is traced by E. Dhorme (Job, 76) to a root לָעָה (la&apos;ah), cognate to an Arabic root meaning &quot;to chatter.&quot; He shows how modern Hebrew has a meaning for the word &quot;to stammer out.&quot; But that does not really fit Job&apos;s outbursts. The idea in the context is rather that of speaking wildly, rashly, or charged with grief. This would trace the word to a hollow or geminate word and link it to Arabic &quot;talk wildly&quot; (see D. J. A. Clines, Job [WBC], 158). In the older works the verb was taken from a geminate root meaning &quot;to suck&quot; or &quot;to swallow&quot; (cf. KJV), but that yields a very difficult sense to the line.

1 tn The word צָבָא (tsava&apos;) is actually &quot;army&quot;; it can be used for the hard service of military service as well as other toil. As a military term it would include the fixed period of duty (the time) and the hard work (toil). Job here is considering the lot of all humans, not just himself. 2 tn The שָׂכִיר (sakhir) is a hired man, either a man who works for wages, or a mercenary soldier (Jer 46:21). The latter sense may be what is intended here in view of the parallelism, although the next verse seems much broader.

3 tn This term עֶבֶד (&apos;eved) is the servant or the slave. He is compelled to work through the day, in the heat; but he longs for evening, when he can rest from the slavery. 4 tn The expression יִשְׁאַף־צֵל (yish&apos;af tsel, &quot;longing for the evening shadow&quot;) could also be taken as a relative clause (without the relative pronoun): &quot;as a servant [who] longs for the evening shadow&quot; (see GKC 487 §155.g). In either case, the expressions in v. 2 emphasize the point of the comparison, which will be summed up in v. 3. 5 tn The two verbs in this verse stress the eager expectation and waiting. The first, שָׁאַף (sha&apos;af), means &quot;to long for; to desire&quot;; and the second, קָוָה (qavah), has the idea of &quot;to hope for; to look for; to wait.&quot; The words would give the sense that the servant or hired man had the longing on his mind all day. 6 tn The word פֹּעַל (po&apos;al) means &quot;work.&quot; But here the word should be taken as a metonymy, meaning the pay for the work that he has done (compare Jer 22:13).

7 tn &quot;Thus&quot; indicates a summary of vv. 1 and 2: like the soldier, the mercenary, and the slave, Job has labored through life and looks forward to death. 8 tn The form is the Hophal perfect of נָחַל (nakhal): &quot;I have been made to inherit,&quot; or more simply, &quot;I have inherited.&quot; The form occurs only here. The LXX must have confused the letters or sounds, a ו (vav) for the ן (nun), for it reads &quot;I have endured.&quot; As a passive the form technically has two accusatives (see GKC 388 §121.c). Job&apos;s point is that his sufferings have been laid on him by another, and so he has inherited them. 9 tn The word is שָׁוְא (shav&apos;, &quot;vanity, deception, nothingness, futility&quot;). His whole life - marked here in months to show its brevity - has been futile. E. Dhorme (Job, 98) suggests the meaning &quot;disillusionment,&quot; explaining that it marks the deceptive nature of mortal life. The word describes life as hollow, insubstantial. 10 tn &quot;Sorrow&quot; is עָמָל (&apos;amal), used in 3:10. It denotes anxious toil, labor, troublesome effort. It may be that the verse expresses the idea that the nights are when the pains of his disease are felt the most. The months are completely wasted; the nights are agonizing. 11 tn The verb is literally &quot;they have appointed&quot;; the form with no expressed subject is to be interpreted as a passive (GKC 460 §144.g). It is therefore not necessary to repoint the verb to make it passive. The word means &quot;to number; to count,&quot; and so &quot;to determine; to allocate.&quot;

1 sn This speech of Bildad ignores Job&apos;s attack on his friends and focuses rather on Job&apos;s comments about God&apos;s justice. Bildad cannot even imagine saying that God is unjust. The only conclusion open to him is that Job&apos;s family brought this on themselves, and so the only recourse is for Job to humble himself and make supplication to God. To make his point, Bildad will appeal to the wisdom of the ancients, for his theology is traditional. The speech has three parts: vv. 2-7 form his affirmation of the justice of God; vv. 8-19 are his appeal to the wisdom of the ancients, and vv. 20-22 are his summation. See N. C. Habel, &quot;Appeal to Ancient Tradition as a Literary Form,&quot; ZAW 88 (1976): 253-72; W. A. Irwin, &quot;The First Speech of Bildad,&quot; ZAW 51 (1953): 205-16.

2 sn &quot;These things&quot; refers to all of Job&apos;s speech, the general drift of which seems to Bildad to question the justice of God. 3 tn The second colon of the verse simply says &quot;and a strong wind the words of your mouth.&quot; The simplest way to treat this is to make it an independent nominal sentence: &quot;the words of your mouth are a strong wind.&quot; Some have made it parallel to the first by apposition, understanding &quot;how long&quot; to do double duty. The line beginning with the ו (vav) can also be subordinated as a circumstantial clause, as here. 4 tn The word כַּבִּיר (kabbir, &quot;great&quot;) implies both abundance and greatness. Here the word modifies &quot;wind&quot;; the point of the analogy is that Job&apos;s words are full of sound but without solid content. 5 tn See, however, G. R. Driver&apos;s translation, &quot;the breath of one who is mighty are the words of your mouth&quot; (&quot;Hebrew Studies,&quot; JRAS 1948: 170).

6 tn The Piel verb יְעַוֵּת (yÿ&apos;avvet) means &quot;to bend; to cause to swerve from the norm; to deviate; to pervert.&quot; The LXX renders the first colon as &quot;will the Lord be unjust when he judges?&quot; 7 tn The first word is מִשְׁפָּת (mishpat, &quot;justice&quot;). It can mean an act of judgment, place of judgment, or what is just, that is, the outcome of the decision. It basically describes an umpire&apos;s decision. The parallel word is צֶדֶק (tsedeq, &quot;righteousness,&quot; or &quot;what is right&quot;). The basic idea here is that which conforms to the standard, what is right. See S. H. Scholnick, &quot;The Meaning of Mishpat in the Book of Job,&quot; JBL 101 (1982): 521-29. 8 tn Some commentators think that the second verb should be changed in order to avoid the repetition of the same word and to reflect the different words in the versions. The suggestion is to read יְעַוֵּה (yÿ&apos;avveh) instead; this would mean &quot;to cause someone to deviate,&quot; for the root means &quot;to bend.&quot; The change is completely unwarranted; the LXX probably chose different words for stylistic reasons (see D. J. A. Clines, Job [WBC], 198). The repetition in the Hebrew text is a common type; it strengthens the enormity of the charge Job seems to be making.

1 sn This speech of Job in response to Bildad falls into two large sections, chs. 9 and 10. In ch. 9 he argues that God&apos;s power and majesty prevent him from establishing his integrity in his complaint to God. And in ch. 10 Job tries to discover in God&apos;s plan the secret of his afflictions. The speech seems to continue what Job was saying to Eliphaz more than it addresses Bildad. See K. Fullerton, &quot;On Job 9 and 10,&quot; JBL 53 (1934): 321-49.

2 tn The adverb אָמְנָם (&apos;omnam, &quot;in truth&quot;) is characteristic of the Book of Job (12:2; 19:4; 34:12; 36:4). The friends make commonplace statements, general truths, and Job responds with &quot;truly I know this is so.&quot; Job knows as much about these themes as his friends do. 3 sn The interrogative is used to express what is an impossibility. 4 tn The attempt to define אֱנוֹשׁ (&apos;enosh) as &quot;weak&quot; or &quot;mortal&quot; man is not compelling. Such interpretations are based on etymological links without the clear support of usage (an issue discussed by J. Barr, Comparative Philology and the Text of the Old Testament). This seems to be a poetic word for &quot;human&quot; (the only nonpoetic use is in 2 Chr 14:10). 5 tn The preposition is אִם (&apos;im, &quot;with, before, in the presence of&quot;). This is more specific than מִן (min) in 4:17. 6 sn The point of Job&apos;s rhetorical question is that man cannot be justified as against God, because God is too powerful and too clever - he controls the universe. He is discussing now the question that Eliphaz raised in 4:17. Peake observes that Job is raising the question of whether something is right because God says it is right, or that God declares it right because it is right.

7 tn Some commentators take God to be the subject of this verb, but it is more likely that it refers to the mortal who tries to challenge God in a controversy. The verb is used of Job in 13:3. 8 tn The verb רִיב (riv) is a common one; it has the idea of &quot;contention; dispute; legal dispute or controversy; go to law.&quot; With the preposition אִם (&apos;im) the idea must be &quot;to contend with&quot; or &quot;to dispute with.&quot; The preposition reflects the prepositional phrase &quot;with God&quot; in v. 2, supporting the view that man is the subject. 9 tn This use of the imperfect as potential imperfect assumes that the human is the subject, that in a dispute with God he could not answer one of God&apos;s questions (for which see the conclusion of the book when God questions Job). On the other hand, if the interpretation were that God does not answer the demands of mortals, then a simple progressive imperfect would be required. In support of this is the frustration of Job that God does not answer him.

1 tn The Hebrew has נַפְשִׁי (nafshi), usually rendered &quot;my soul.&quot; 2 tn The verb is pointed like a Qal form but is originally a Niphal from קוּט (qut). Some wish to connect the word to Akkadian cognates for a meaning &quot;I am in anguish&quot;; but the meaning &quot;I am weary&quot; fits the passage well. 3 tn The verb עָזַב (&apos;azav) means &quot;to abandon.&quot; It may have an extended meaning of &quot;to let go&quot; or &quot;to let slip.&quot; But the expression &quot;abandon to myself&quot; means to abandon all restraint and give free course to the complaint.

4 tn The negated jussive is the Hiphil jussive of רָשַׁע (rasha&apos;); its meaning then would be literally &quot;do not declare me guilty.&quot; The negated jussive stresses the immediacy of the request. 5 tn The Hiphil imperative of יָדַע (yada&apos;) would more literally be &quot;cause me to know.&quot; It is a plea for God to help him understand the afflictions. 6 tn The verb is רִיב (riv), meaning &quot;to dispute; to contend; to strive; to quarrel&quot; - often in the legal sense. The precise words chosen in this verse show that the setting is legal. The imperfect verb here is progressive, expressing what is currently going on.

7 tn Or &quot;Does it give you pleasure?&quot; The expression could also mean, &quot;Is it profitable for you?&quot; or &quot;Is it fitting for you?&quot; 8 tn The construction uses כִּי (ki) with the imperfect verb - &quot;that you oppress.&quot; Technically, this clause serves as the subject, and &quot;good&quot; is the predicate adjective. In such cases one often uses an English infinitive to capture the point: &quot;Is it good for you to oppress?&quot; The LXX changes the meaning considerably: &quot;Is it good for you if I am unrighteous, for you have disowned the work of your hands.&quot; 9 tn Heb &quot;that you despise.&quot; 10 tn Now, in the second half of the verse, there is a change in the structure. The conjunction on the preposition followed by the perfect verb represents a circumstantial clause. 11 tn The Hiphil of the verb יָפַע (yafa&apos;) means &quot;shine.&quot; In this context the expression &quot;you shine upon&quot; would mean &quot;have a glowing expression,&quot; be radiant, or smile.

1 sn Zophar begins with a strong rebuke of Job with a wish that God would speak (2-6); he then reflects for a few verses on the unsearchable wisdom of God (7-12); and finally, he advises Job that the way to restoration is repentance (13-20).

2 tc The LXX, Targum Job, Symmachus, and Vulgate all assume that the vocalization of רֹב (rov, &quot;abundance&quot;) should be רַב (rav, &quot;great&quot;): &quot;great of words.&quot; This would then mean &quot;one who is abundant of words,&quot; meaning, &quot;a man of many words,&quot; and make a closer parallel to the second half. But the MT makes good sense as it stands. tn There is no article or demonstrative with the word; it has been added here simply to make a smoother connection between the chapters. 3 tn The Niphal verb יֵעָנֶה (ye&apos;aneh, &quot;he answered&quot;) would normally require a personal subject, but &quot;abundance&quot; functions as the subject in this sentence. The nuance of the imperfect is obligatory. 4 tn The word is supplied here also for clarification. 5 tn The bound construction &quot;man of lips&quot; means &quot;a boaster&quot; or &quot;proud talker&quot; (attributive genitive; and see GKC 417 §128.t). Zophar is saying that Job pours out this stream of words, but he is still not right. 6 tn The word is literally &quot;be right, righteous.&quot; The idea of being right has appeared before for this word (cf. 9:15). The point here is that just because Job talks a lot does not mean he is right or will be shown to be right through it all.

7 tn The word means &quot;chatter, pratings, boastings&quot; (see Isa 16:6; Jer 48:30). 8 tn The verb חָרַשׁ (kharash) in the Hiphil means &quot;to silence&quot; (41:4); here it functions in a causative sense, &quot;reduce to silence.&quot; 9 tn The form מַכְלִם (makhlim, &quot;humiliating, mocking&quot;) is the Hiphil participle. The verb כָּלַם (kalam) has the meaning &quot;cover with shame, insult&quot; (Job 20:3). 10 tn The construction shows the participle to be in the circumstantial clause: &quot;will you mock - and [with] no one rebuking.&quot;

1 sn This long speech of Job falls into three parts: in 12:2-25 Job expresses his resentment at his friends&apos; attitude of superiority and acknowledges the wisdom of God; then, in 13:1-28 Job expresses his determination to reason with God, expresses his scorn for his friends&apos; advice, and demands to know what his sins are; and finally, in 14:1-22 Job laments the brevity of life and the finality of death.

2 tn The expression &quot;you are the people&quot; is a way of saying that the friends hold the popular opinion - they represent it. The line is sarcastic. Commentators do not think the parallelism is served well by this, and so offer changes for &quot;people.&quot; Some have suggested &quot;you are complete&quot; (based on Arabic), &quot;you are the strong one&quot; (based on Ugaritic), etc. J. A. Davies tried to solve the difficulty by making the second clause in the verse a paratactic relative clause: &quot;you are the people with whom wisdom will die&quot; (&quot;Note on Job 12:2,&quot; VT 25 [1975]: 670-71). 3 sn The sarcasm of Job admits their claim to wisdom, as if no one has it besides them. But the rest of his speech will show that they do not have a monopoly on it.

4 tn The word is literally &quot;heart,&quot; meaning a mind or understanding. 5 tn Because this line is repeated in 13:2, many commentators delete it from this verse (as does the LXX). The Syriac translates נֹפֵל (nofel) as &quot;little,&quot; and the Vulgate &quot;inferior.&quot; Job is saying that he does not fall behind them in understanding. 6 tn Heb &quot;With whom are not such things as these?&quot; The point is that everyone knows the things that these friends have been saying - they are commonplace.

1 sn Chapter 13 records Job&apos;s charges against his friends for the way they used their knowledge (1-5), his warning that God would find out their insincerity (6-12), and his pleading of his cause to God in which he begs for God to remove his hand from him and that he would not terrify him with his majesty and that he would reveal the sins that caused such great suffering (13-28). 2 tn Hebrew has כֹּל (kol, &quot;all&quot;); there is no reason to add anything to the text to gain a meaning &quot;all this.&quot;

3 tn Heb &quot;Like your knowledge&quot;; in other words Job is saying that his knowledge is like their knowledge. 4 tn The pronoun makes the subject emphatic and stresses the contrast: &quot;I know - I also.&quot; 5 tn The verb &quot;fall&quot; is used here as it was in Job 4:13 to express becoming lower than someone, i.e., inferior.

6 tn The verb is simply the Piel imperfect אֲדַבֵּר (&apos;adabber, &quot;I speak&quot;). It should be classified as a desiderative imperfect, saying, &quot;I desire to speak.&quot; This is reinforced with the verb &quot;to wish, desire&quot; in the second half of the verse. 7 tn The Hebrew title for God here is אֶל־שַׁדַּי (&apos;el shadday, &quot;El Shaddai&quot;). 8 tn The infinitive absolute functions here as the direct object of the verb &quot;desire&quot; (see GKC 340 §113.b). 9 tn The infinitive הוֹכֵחַ (hokheakh) is from the verb יָכַח (yakhakh), which means &quot;to argue, plead, debate.&quot; It has the legal sense here of arguing a case (cf. 5:17).

1 sn In the first round of speeches, Eliphaz had emphasized the moral perfection of God, Bildad his unwavering justice, and Zophar his omniscience. 2 tn The Hebrew is דַעַת־רוּחַ (da&apos;at-ruakh). This means knowledge without any content, vain knowledge. 3 tn The image is rather graphic. 5 tn The infinitive absolute in this place is functioning either as an explanatory adverb or as a finite verb. sn Eliphaz draws on Job&apos;s claim with this word (cf. 1 tn The verb חָבַל (khaval, &quot;to act badly&quot;) in the Piel means &quot;to ruin.&quot; The Pual translation with &quot;my spirit&quot; as the subject means &quot;broken&quot; in the sense of finished (not in the sense of humbled as in Ps 51). 2 tn The verb זָעַךְ (za&apos;aq, equivalent of Aramaic דָעַק [da&apos;aq]) means &quot;to be extinguished.&quot; It only occurs here in the Hebrew. 3 tn The plural &quot;graves&quot; could be simply an intensification, a plural of extension (see GKC 397 §124.c), or a reference to the graveyard. Coverdale had: &quot;I am harde at deathes dore.&quot; The Hebrew expression simply reads &quot;graves for me.&quot; It probably means that graves await him.

4 tn The noun is the abstract noun, &quot;mockery.&quot; It indicates that he is the object of derision. But many commentators either change the word to &quot;mockers&quot; (Tur-Sinai, NEB), or argue that the form in the text is a form of the participle (Gordis). 5 tn E. Dhorme (Job, 243) interprets the preposition to mean &quot;aimed at me.&quot; 6 tn The meaning of הַמְּרוֹתָם (hammÿrotam) is unclear, and the versions offer no help. If the MT is correct, it would probably be connected to מָרָה (marah, &quot;to be rebellious&quot;) and the derived form something like &quot;hostility; provocation.&quot; But some commentators suggest it should be related to מָרֹרוֹת (marorot, &quot;bitter things&quot;). Others have changed both the noun and the verb to obtain something like &quot;My eye is weary of their contentiousness&quot; (Holscher), or mine eyes are wearied by your stream of peevish complaints&quot; (G. R. Driver, &quot;Problems in the Hebrew text of Job,&quot; VTSup 3 [1955]: 78). There is no alternative suggestion that is compelling.

7 tn The MT has two imperatives: &quot;Lay down, pledge me, with me.&quot; Most commentators think that the second imperative should be a noun, and take it to say, &quot;Lay my pledge with/beside you.&quot; A. B. Davidson (Job, 126) suggests that the first verb means &quot;give a pledge,&quot; and so the two similar verbs would be emphatic: &quot;Give a pledge, be my surety.&quot; Other than such a change (which would involve changing the vowels) one would have to interpret similarly by seeing the imperatives as a kind of hendiadys, with the main emphasis being on the second imperative, &quot;make a pledge.&quot; 8 sn The idiom is &quot;to strike the hand.&quot; Here the wording is a little different, &quot;Who is he that will strike himself into my hand?&quot;

1 sn Bildad attacks Job with less subtlety than Eliphaz. He describes the miserable existence of the wicked, indicating that it is the proof of sin. His speech falls into two main parts: why is Job so contemptuous toward his friends (Job 18:2-4), and the fate of the wicked (18:5-21). On this chapter see N. M. Sarna, &quot;The Mythological Background of Job 18,&quot; JBL 82 (1963): 315-18; and W. A. Irwin, &quot;Job&apos;s Redeemer,&quot; JBL 81 (1962): 217-29.

2 tn The verb is plural, and so most commentators make it singular. But it seems from the context that Bildad is addressing all of them, and not just Job. 3 tn The construction is קִנְצֵי לְמִלִּין (qintse lÿmillin), which is often taken to be &quot;end of words,&quot; as if the word was from קֵץ (qets, &quot;end&quot;). But a plural of &quot;end&quot; is not found in the OT. Some will link the word to Arabic qanasa, &quot;to hunt; to give chase,&quot; to get an interpretation of &quot;snares for words.&quot; But E. Dhorme (Job, 257) objects that this does not fit the speech of Bildad (as well as it might Job&apos;s). He finds a cognate qinsu, &quot;fetters, shackles,&quot; and reads &quot;how long will you put shackles on words.&quot; But G. R. Driver had pointed out that this cognate does not exist (&quot;Problems in the Hebrew text of Job,&quot; VTSup 3 [1955]: 72-93). So it would be preferable to take the reading &quot;ends&quot; and explain the ן (nun) as from a Aramaizing by-form. This is supported by 11QtgJob that uses סוֹף (sof, &quot;end&quot;). On the construction, GKC 421 §130.a explains this as a use of the construct in rapid narrative to connect the words; in such cases a preposition is on the following noun. 4 tn The imperfect verb, again plural, would be here taken in the nuance of instruction, or a modal nuance of obligation. So Bildad is telling his listeners to be intelligent. This would be rather cutting in the discourse. 5 tn Heb &quot;afterward.&quot;

6 tn The verb נִטְמִינוּ (nitminu) has been explained from different roots. Some take it from תָּמֵא (tame&apos;, &quot;to be unclean&quot;), and translate it &quot;Why should we be unclean in your eyes?&quot; Most would connect it to טָמַם (tamam, &quot;to stop up&quot;), meaning &quot;to be stupid&quot; in the Niphal. Another suggestion is to follow the LXX and read from דָּמַם (damam, &quot;to be reduced to silence&quot;). Others take it from דָּמָּה (damah) with a meaning &quot;to be like.&quot; But what is missing is the term of comparison - like what? Various suggestions have been made, but all are simply conjectures.

1 sn Job is completely stunned by Bildad&apos;s speech, and feels totally deserted by God and his friends. Yet from his despair a new hope emerges with a stronger faith. Even though he knows he will die in his innocence, he knows that God will vindicate him and that he will be conscious of the vindication. There are four parts to this reply: Job&apos;s impatience with the speeches of his friends (2-6), God&apos;s abandonment of Job and his attack (7-12), Job&apos;s forsaken state and appeal to his friends (13-22), and Job&apos;s confidence that he will be vindicated (23-29).

2 tn Heb &quot;torment my soul,&quot; with &quot;soul&quot; representing the self or individual. The MT has a verb from יָגָה (yagah, &quot;to afflict; to torment&quot;). This is supported by the versions. But the LXX has &quot;to tire&quot; which is apparently from יָגַע (yaga&apos;). The form in the MT is unusual because it preserves the final (original) yod in the Hiphil (see GKC 214 §75.gg). So this unusual form has been preserved, and is the correct reading. A modal nuance for the imperfect fits best here: &quot;How long do you intend to do this?&quot; 3 tn The MT has דָּכָא (dakha&apos;), &quot;to crush&quot; in the Piel. The LXX, however, has a more general word which means &quot;to destroy.&quot; 4 tn The LXX adds to the verse: &quot;only know that the Lord has dealt with me thus.&quot;

5 sn The number &quot;ten&quot; is a general expression to convey that this has been done often (see Gen 31:7; Num 14:22). 6 tn The Hiphil of the verb כָּלַם (kalam) means &quot;outrage; insult; shame.&quot; The verbs in this verse are prefixed conjugations, and may be interpreted as preterites if the reference is to the past time. But since the action is still going on, progressive imperfects work well. 7 tn The second half of the verse uses two verbs, the one dependent on the other. It could be translated &quot;you are not ashamed to attack me&quot; (see GKC 385-86 §120.c), or &quot;you attack me shamelessly.&quot; The verb חָכַר (hakhar) poses some difficulties for both the ancient versions and the modern commentators. The verb seems to be cognate to Arabic hakara, &quot;to oppress; to ill-treat.&quot; This would mean that there has been a transformation of ח (khet) to ה (he). Three Hebrew mss actually have the ח (khet). This has been widely accepted; other suggestions are irrelevant.
